Competitive intelligence sources are the people, records, and data feeds that show what your rivals are doing and why customers might choose them. Most are already within reach. Your sales calls, supplier conversations, customer reviews, job boards, and public filings all qualify.

Primary sources are information you collect firsthand. Secondary sources are information someone else has already collected or published. Strong programs use both, plus a third group called internal intelligence, which covers what your own teams already hear.
Reviews, competitor websites, SEC filings, patents, news, job postings
Use secondary sources to spot what changed. Use primary sources to learn why it matters.
A new market segment calls for industry associations, conferences, filings, and a market survey.
People are your richest primary sources because they explain why buyers choose one company over another. Five groups are the most productive to ask:
Public filings and patents
9. Public filings and patents

For US companies, public filings and patent records rank among the most reliable secondary sources. Public companies must file reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and anyone can read them for free in EDGAR, the SEC’s
public filing database
Public websites, filings, patents, and press releases

Public sources such as SEC filings, patents, websites, reviews, and press releases are legal to use. Risk begins when someone obtains trade secrets through deception, theft, or a breach of confidentiality. This is general information, so ask an attorney to review your policy.
